{"kind":"tool","id":"gmERvY5qzbQ","toolName":"str_replace","input":{"path":"src/world/facade.js","replacements":[{"oldString":"    // iron cresting on the runs that are slate, the way a mansard ridge is
    // finished: a rail on short standards, one every 0.55 m. It reads as a fine
    // dark sawtooth against the sky, which is exactly its job in the reference.
    for (const [r0, r1] of runs) {
      const rail = g3(r1 - r0, 0.06, 0.06);
      rail.translate((r0 + r1) / 2, MANSARD.y1 + 0.62, MANSARD.p1 + 0.04);
      placeOnWall(rail, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
      B.iron.push(rail);
      for (let u = r0 + 0.28; u < r1 - 0.2; u += 0.55) {
        const bar = g3(0.045, 0.50, 0.045);
        bar.translate(u, MANSARD.y1 + 0.36, MANSARD.p1 + 0.04);
        placeOnWall(bar, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
        B.iron.push(bar);
      }
    }
  }","newString":"    // iron cresting on the runs that are slate, the way a mansard ridge is
    // finished: a rail on short standards, one every 0.55 m. It reads as a fine
    // dark sawtooth against the sky, which is exactly its job in the reference.
    for (const [r0, r1] of runs) {
      const rail = g3(r1 - r0, 0.06, 0.06);
      rail.translate((r0 + r1) / 2, MANSARD.y1 + 0.62, MANSARD.p1 + 0.04);
      placeOnWall(rail, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
      B.iron.push(rail);
      for (let u = r0 + 0.28; u < r1 - 0.2; u += 0.55) {
        const bar = g3(0.045, 0.50, 0.045);
        bar.translate(u, MANSARD.y1 + 0.36, MANSARD.p1 + 0.04);
        placeOnWall(bar, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
        B.iron.push(bar);
      }
    }

    // Mansard ridge cresting + finial row, matching the reference elevation.
    // A mansard's iron ridge runs along the roof's top edge (the slate's outer
    // lip), not down the centre of the slope. It is a thin flat rail carried on
    // short standards, and at each corner it is closed by a small turned finial
    // so the cresting reads as one continuous iron band around the roof.
    const ridgeY = MANSARD.y1;
    const ridgeOff = MANSARD.p1 + 0.04;
    const ridgeRailW = f.ub - f.ua + 0.28;
    const ridgeRail = g3(ridgeRailW, 0.05, 0.09);
    ridgeRail.translate((f.ua + f.ub) / 2, ridgeY + 0.04, ridgeOff);
    placeOnWall(ridgeRail, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
    B.iron.push(ridgeRail);
    // short standards under the ridge rail, one every 0.55 m
    for (let u = f.ua + 0.34; u < f.ub - 0.30; u += 0.55) {
      const st = g3(0.045, 0.055, 0.045);
      st.translate(u, ridgeY + 0.025, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(st, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
      B.iron.push(st);
    }
    // finial row at the ridge ends: the cresting is closed with a small ball on
    // a short stem at each end of the run, matching the finial each gable ridge
    // already carries.
    const finStem = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.030, 0.030, 0.30, 6);
    const finBall = new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.075, 8, 6);
    for (const endU of [f.ua, f.ub]) {
      finStem.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.16, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(finStem, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
      B.iron.push(finStem);
      finBall.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.34, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(finBall, f.axis, f.line, f.out);
      B.iron.push(finBall);
    }
  }","allowMultiple":false}]}}

function mansardRidgeCresting(B, arch, gf) {

  const f4 = LEVELS.find((l) => l.id === 'F4');
  const winsOn = (axis, line) => arch.windows.filter((w) =>
    w.level === 'F4' && w.axis === axis && Math.abs(w.c - line) < 0.02);

  // The same ridge rail, standards and end finials as the per-face cresting
  // already built in mansard(), recomputed for every face that still carries
  // slate at the top. The result is one closed iron band around the mansard
  // perimeter, with a finial at each corner.
  const ridgeY = MANSARD.y1;
  const ridgeOff = MANSARD.p1 + 0.04;

  const buildRun = (axis, line, out, ua, ub) => {
    const railLen = ub - ua;
    if (railLen < 0.05) return;
    const rail = g3(railLen, 0.05, 0.09);
    rail.translate((ua + ub) / 2, ridgeY + 0.04, ridgeOff);
    placeOnWall(rail, axis, line, out);
    B.iron.push(rail);
    for (let u = ua + 0.34; u < ub - 0.30; u += 0.55) {
      const st = g3(0.045, 0.055, 0.045);
      st.translate(u, ridgeY + 0.025, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(st, axis, line, out);
      B.iron.push(st);
    }
    const finStem = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.030, 0.030, 0.30, 6);
    const finBall = new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.075, 8, 6);
    for (const endU of [ua, ub]) {
      finStem.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.16, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(finStem, axis, line, out);
      B.iron.push(finStem);
      finBall.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.34, ridgeOff);
      placeOnWall(finBall, axis, line, out);
      B.iron.push(finBall);
    }
  };

  const south = fp.x0 < 0 && fp.x1 > 0;
  const north = fp.x0 < 0 && fp.x1 > 0;
  const east = fp.z0 < 0 && fp.z1 > 0;
  const west = fp.z0 < 0 && fp.z1 > 0;

  // South face (front) — skip the gable bay that the mansard slate already
  // stops at, so the cresting only runs on the slate strips beside the gable.
  if (south) {
    const zLine = fp.z1;
    const out = 1;
    const baseRuns = mansardFace(B, 'x', zLine, out, fp.x0, fp.x1, winsOn('x', zLine), f4.y, [MANSARD_GABLE]);

  // North face
  if (north) {
    const zLine = fp.z0;
    const out = -1;

    const xLine = fp.x1;
    const out = 1;
    const baseRuns = mansardFace(B, 'z', xLine, out, fp.z0, fp.z1, winsOn('z', xLine), f4.y, [[5.3, 11.3]]);
    for (const [r0, r1] of baseRuns) buildRun('z', xLine, out, r0, r1);
  }
  // West face
  if (west) {
    const xLine = fp.x0;
    const out = -1;
    const baseRuns = mansardFace(B, 'z', xLine, out, fp.z0, fp.z1, winsOn('z', xLine), f4.y, [[6.9, 12.3]]);
    for (const [r0, r1] of baseRuns) buildRun('z', xLine, out, r0, r1);
  }

  // ridge cresting band over the gable: the mansard's iron ridge closes across
  // the front gable opening the same way the slate ridge is capped, so the
  // centerline ridge does not end in a raw slate edge over the blind arch.
  const gableRailW = 10.6;
  const gableRail = g3(gableRailW, 0.05, 0.09);
  gableRail.translate(0, ridgeY + 0.04, ridgeOff);
  placeOnWall(gableRail, 'x', fp.z1, 1);
  B.iron.push(gableRail);
  for (let u = -5.0; u <= 5.0; u += 0.55) {
    const st = g3(0.045, 0.055, 0.045);
    st.translate(u, ridgeY + 0.025, ridgeOff);
    placeOnWall(st, 'x', fp.z1, 1);
    B.iron.push(st);
  }
  const gableFinStem = new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.030, 0.030, 0.30, 6);
  const gableFinBall = new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.075, 8, 6);
  for (const endU of [-5.3, 5.3]) {
    gableFinStem.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.16, ridgeOff);
    placeOnWall(gableFinStem, 'x', fp.z1, 1);
    B.iron.push(gableFinStem);
    gableFinBall.translate(endU, ridgeY + 0.34, ridgeOff);
    placeOnWall(gableFinBall, 'x', fp.z1, 1);
    B.iron.push(gableFinBall);
  }

function noiseCanvas(size, base, spread, seed) {
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = c.height = size;
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = `rgb(${base},${base},${base})`;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, size, size);
  // coarse blotches first, then fine grain: roughness varies at two scales on
  // any real glazed or painted surface
  let s = seed;
  const rnd = () => (s = (s * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  for (let i = 0; i < 220; i++) {
    const r = 4 + rnd() * size * 0.16;
    const v = base + (rnd() - 0.5) * spread * 2;
    const x = rnd() * size, y = rnd() * size;
    ctx.fillStyle = `rgb(${v|0},${v|0},${v|0})`;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(x, y, r, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();
  }
  return c;

# Running this workspace

Two different things live here and they must not be confused:

* `npm run dev` (root `index.html` + `src/`) — the **old** game build. It is not
  the rebuild and it is not what the preview should show.
* `Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/` — the **rebuild**: the house authored in
  Blender, exported to a GLB, and walked in a first-person viewer.

## 1. Build the house (Blender, headless)

```bash
B="/c/Program Files/Blender Foundation/Blender 4.2/blender.exe"

# the whole set: 50 rooms over 4 storeys plus the silong and 12 tunnel areas,
# 58 doors/arches, 68 windows, 4 stair runs
"$B" -b --factory-startup \
  --python Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/_build/build_house.py

# open the four doors that lead OUTSIDE, then re-export the GLB
"$B" -b Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/SILID_House_v1.blend \
  --python Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/_build/cut_out_doors.py
```

Step 2 is not optional. Without it the exported walls arrive sealed: the front
door is a solid panel with a door casing in front of it, and the walkthrough
cannot leave the house.

**Use `cut_out_doors.py`, not `cut_openings.py`.** The latter subtracts every
opening with a boolean, and the walls are one mesh made of hundreds of touching
boxes: the EXACT solver welds the shared faces and dissolves the ones it thinks
are internal, so 30 openings punched 193 undeclared holes through the front
facade (215 on the east side) — walls you could see through everywhere except
at the door. `cut_out_doors.py` touches only the faces lying across the four
outside doors and clips them by hand, so the facade cannot spring leaks.

**The house is not in the plan's frame.** It was rotated +90° about X for glTF:
plan `(x, y, z)` lives at world `(x, -z, y)`, so the front wall sits at
`world y = +7.15` and there is no wall at `world z = -7` at all. Any script that
places geometry in plan coordinates will silently miss. `cut_out_doors.py`
converts explicitly, and `probe_openings.py` measures the result:

```bash
# which declared openings are still walled up? (blend, then the exported GLB)
"$B" -b Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/SILID_House_v1.blend \
  --python Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/_build/probe_openings.py
"$B" -b --factory-startup \
  --python Blender/AssetLibrary/Working/House/_build/probe_openings.py -- --glb
```

# SILID — REALISTIC MANSION RECONSTRUCTION AND IMMERSIVE GAMEPLAY OVERHAUL
## Build a Believable, Detailed, Physically Constructed Mansion Inspired by Realistic First-Person Exploration Games

### PROJECT OBJECTIVE

Improve SILID's mansion architecture, interior realism, environmental materials, furniture, and gameplay.

I want the mansion to achieve the level of environmental realism found in high-quality first-person exploration and horror games: believable room proportions, physically convincing architecture, detailed everyday objects, natural material variation, coherent lighting, and immersive exploration.

The visual reference I have in mind features realistic indoor environments with detailed rooms, kitchens, bathrooms, laundry areas, tiled floors, wooden beams, furniture, appliances, and ordinary household objects. The environments feel physically constructed and naturally furnished rather than assembled from simple cubes.

The reference also demonstrates the value of first-person exploration through believable spaces, where objects and rooms can be inspected at close range and the environment feels like a real place.

Use these qualities as inspiration. Do not copy another game's proprietary assets, characters, maps, or distinctive content.

**I will not provide the reference video. You must work from this written description, your own internet research, and the existing SILID project.**

My goal is not to create a generic mansion. SILID must retain its own identity as a psychological horror game set in an old, remote Filipino mansion.

The project uses Three.js, Vite, and JavaScript. Do not migrate it to Unreal Engine.

# PHASE 1 — INSPECT THE EXISTING GAME

Before changing anything, inspect the actual project files and running game.

Identify:
- How the mansion geometry is created or loaded.
- How floors, ceilings, walls, doors, windows, stairs, and railings are constructed.
- How furniture and household props are modeled.
- How materials and textures are loaded and assigned.
- How lighting, shadows, and the first-person camera work.
- How collision, interaction, inventory, hiding, puzzles, and enemy behavior are implemented.

Back up affected files before editing. Reuse good existing assets and systems wherever possible.

Do not rebuild the entire game blindly. Identify the actual causes of poor realism and correct them systematically.

# PHASE 2 — ARCHITECTURAL REALISM

The mansion must feel like a real building designed and constructed by people.

## Floors and ceilings
- Give floor slabs convincing three-dimensional thickness.
- Model visible slab edges and undersides correctly.
- Ensure ceilings and upper floors connect naturally to walls and supporting structures.
- Remove paper-thin floors, floating slabs, unexplained gaps, and intersecting geometry.
- Use appropriate construction for timber, concrete, or masonry surfaces.
- Ensure floor openings are correctly sized for stairs and other architectural features.

## Circular staircase
- Correct the proportions of treads, risers, landings, and railings.
- Make the staircase connect naturally to every intended storey.
- Ensure its central support and surrounding structure make architectural sense.
- Prevent the steps from intersecting floors or terminating in inaccessible spaces.
- Maintain sufficient headroom and walking clearance.
- Make the underside and surrounding floor edges look like real construction.

## Walls, doors, and windows
- Give walls believable thickness and construction.
- Ensure doorframes, window frames, lintels, sills, and trim fit the openings correctly.
- Remove fake openings, floating trim, overlapping wall surfaces, and visibly unfinished edges.
- Use appropriate materials and proportions for an old Filipino mansion.

Do not hide geometry defects with darkness or decorative objects.

# PHASE 3 — REALISTIC INTERIOR DESIGN

Furnish rooms as though the mansion was genuinely inhabited and later abandoned.

Create coherent layouts for the existing rooms, including the foyer, sala, dining room, kitchen, bedrooms, bathrooms, study, storage areas, utility spaces, basement, and underground areas where those rooms exist in the current design.

Use believable furniture and household objects, including:
- Wooden tables, chairs, beds, cabinets, wardrobes, and aparadors.
- Functional drawers and shelves with real interior cavities.
- Kitchen counters, sinks, utensils, dishes, and storage.
- Bathroom fixtures and realistic tiled surfaces.
- Laundry appliances and utility equipment.
- Old family photographs, personal belongings, religious objects, fans, lamps, and other appropriate Filipino household details.

Every object must have a sensible position, scale, purpose, and relationship to the room.

Do not fill rooms with random decorations. Preserve clear walking routes and enough space for the player to move, inspect objects, and evade enemies.

# PHASE 4 — RESEARCH AND APPLY REALISTIC MATERIALS

Research suitable downloadable materials online instead of guessing or assigning generic textures.

Start with:
- Poly Haven: https://polyhaven.com/textures
- ambientCG: https://ambientcg.com/
- Poly Haven Asphalt 01: https://polyhaven.com/a/asphalt_01
- Poly Haven Worn Asphalt: https://polyhaven.com/a/worn_asphalt
- Poly Haven Mud Forest: https://polyhaven.com/a/mud_forest
- Poly Haven Tree Bark 03: https://polyhaven.com/a/tree_bark_03

Research additional materials appropriate to each surface.

### Mansion materials
Use distinct, believable materials for:
- Aged plaster and painted walls.
- Old timber and wooden flooring.
- Concrete, stone, and exposed masonry.
- Weathered metal and roofing.
- Glass and painted wooden frames.
- Ceramic tiles and bathroom surfaces.
- Damp basement walls and underground masonry.

### Exterior materials
Use:
- Realistic asphalt for the provincial road.
- Gravel and compacted earth for roadside shoulders.
- Natural soil, mud, leaves, grass, and roots for the forest floor.
- Textured tree bark and appropriate foliage.
- Believable dirt and moisture transitions between surfaces.

### PBR implementation
Where supported, use appropriate base-color, normal, roughness, and ambient-occlusion maps.

Ensure:
- Correct UV mapping and real-world texture scale.
- Proper color-space handling.
- Natural roughness and surface response.
- No obvious texture stretching or repetitive tiling.
- No exaggerated bump mapping or unrealistic gloss.

Prefer legitimate assets with documented licenses, including CC0 assets where appropriate. Record asset names, sources, and licenses.

Do not merely provide a list of recommended textures. Integrate suitable materials into the actual game when possible.

# PHASE 5 — REALISTIC FURNITURE AND FUNCTIONAL OBJECTS

Avoid furniture that looks like a group of rectangular primitives.

Improve the geometry, proportions, joints, supports, handles, and materials of existing furniture.

For drawers:
- Model real cavities, bottoms, sides, and front panels.
- Implement correct sliding movement.
- Prevent clipping and intersections.
- Preserve item contents and interaction states.

For the generator:
- Create a coherent machine with a believable housing, ventilation, controls, wiring, connections, and supporting frame.
- Use realistic metal, paint, rust, and wear.
- Preserve existing repair and progression mechanics.

For the phone:
- Use my supplied 3D phone model file as the actual in-game phone.
- Inspect its real format and use the appropriate loader.
- Preserve its geometry and materials where possible.
- Use a 3D model for the physical phone, whether placed in the world or held in first person.
- A separate interface may display readable phone contents, but a flat overlay must not substitute for the physical model.

Preserve existing gameplay functionality while improving these objects.

# PHASE 6 — IMMERSIVE FIRST-PERSON GAMEPLAY

Improve the experience beyond visual quality.

The player should be able to explore the mansion naturally, inspect important objects, discover clues, open appropriate furniture, and understand the space through environmental details.

Implement or refine:
- Functional doors, drawers, cabinets, and other meaningful objects.
- Believable pickup and inventory behavior.
- Hiding inside suitable wardrobes or beneath beds.
- Peeking from hiding places while maintaining realistic visibility restrictions.
- Environmental puzzles based on logical object relationships.
- Meaningful clues and environmental storytelling.
- Appropriate audio feedback for movement, doors, objects, and nearby threats.

Not every decorative item needs an interaction prompt. Every meaningful object should have a deliberate role, while scenery remains unobtrusive.

## Psychological horror

Retain SILID's psychological horror identity and existing Resident concept.

Focus on tension, uncertainty, environmental storytelling, and intelligent enemy behavior rather than constant jump scares.

Improve enemy perception, searching, and responses to player visibility and sound. Ensure hiding spaces and escape routes work physically and fairly.

Do not introduce unrelated creatures or copy another game's signature mechanics or content without adapting them to SILID's story.

# PHASE 7 — LIGHTING AND ATMOSPHERE

Maintain a dark, unsettling nighttime atmosphere with restrained warm lights, cool shadows, believable flashlight illumination, and natural falloff.

The environment should still reveal enough detail for the player to recognize surfaces, geometry, and nearby objects.

Use lighting to enhance realism, not conceal bad models or missing textures.

Avoid:
- Uniformly black surfaces.
- Excessively bright rooms.
- Unnaturally glossy materials.
- Excessive dynamic lights and shadows.
- Fake lighting baked into base-color textures.

# PHASE 8 — PERFORMANCE

My computer has an Intel HD Graphics 4600 integrated GPU and 8 GB RAM.

Keep the game practical to run on this hardware.

Use efficient geometry, shared materials, sensible texture resolutions, appropriate collision meshes, and restrained lighting.

Prioritize good silhouettes, convincing proportions, close-up detail, and correct materials rather than unnecessarily high polygon counts.

Do not sacrifice the entire visual quality by replacing everything with cubes.

# PHASE 9 — IMPLEMENTATION AND TESTING

Work in stages:

1. Inspect and back up the existing project.
2. Audit the mansion architecture and identify the most serious defects.
3. Correct the floors, circular staircase, and structural connections.
4. Improve the material library and texture assignments.
5. Improve furniture and meaningful interactive objects.
6. Refine first-person exploration and psychological horror gameplay.
7. Test movement, collisions, interactions, and floor accessibility.
8. Verify the game in its actual browser runtime.
9. Capture genuine before-and-after screenshots.

Test the environment from the first-person camera, including close inspection of furniture, movement through corridors, views beneath floors, stair traversal, and interaction with the generator and phone.

Preserve existing functionality. Do not claim success based only on generated code or a successful build.

## REQUIRED DELIVERABLES

Provide:
- A summary of the realism principles applied.
- The actual files and assets modified.
- The materials researched and their source links and licenses.
- Screenshots showing the improved architecture, furniture, and representative rooms.
- Results of runtime, collision, interaction, and performance testing.
- A list of remaining issues and unverified features.

## FINAL QUALITY STANDARD

SILID must feel like a believable, physically constructed, lived-in Filipino mansion that has become unsettling through neglect, unexplained events, and psychological horror.

Achieve this through coherent architecture, realistic construction, detailed furniture, appropriate materials, natural object placement, carefully controlled lighting, and immersive first-person gameplay.

Use online research and sound modeling practices to make informed decisions. Preserve SILID's existing identity and working systems. Implement the improvements in the actual project and verify the results.

Search online. Get what you need and download something you can use. And use Blender. I want a very detailed environment.

function pose(room) {
  const [x0, z0, x1, z1] = room.rect;
  const x = x0 + (x1 - x0) * room.at[0];
  const z = z0 + (z1 - z0) * room.at[1];
  const tx = x0 + (x1 - x0) * room.aim[0];
  const tz = z0 + (z1 - z0) * room.aim[1];
  const yaw = Math.atan2(-(tx - x), -(tz - z));
  return { x: +x.toFixed(2), z: +z.toFixed(2), yaw: +yaw.toFixed(3) };
}

I completed one verified realism pass on the live game rather than attempting all nine phases at once. The mansion, its materials and the Blender furniture pipeline already existed and were stronger than first appeared; the real defects were scale, light coverage and a few pieces of dressing.

![Dining room after the pass](reports/realism/tour_after3/dining_s.png)

**What I found and fixed**

Every interior surface was textured at one repeat per metre, although the UVs are laid in metres and the source photographs cover two to three metres. A 7 m wall wore three and a half copies of a 2 m plaster photograph, so rooms read as grids of square panels, and the floorboards repeated three times too often. The real-world sizes were already recorded in the licence table; they are now in the material table and applied at the wall, floor and prop callers ([materials.js](src/world/materials.js), [architecture.js](src/world/architecture.js), [props.js](src/world/props.js)). This also removed a latent bug where a cloned material silently rewrote the tiling of every other mesh sharing its textures.

Several room kinds were dressed but never lit — dining, gallery, music room and others. With the torch on, the dining room still read as an empty box. Every otherwise-unlit room now gets a pendant (canopy, shade and bulb merged into the room's prop mesh) with its point light just under the shade. Wall tile is laid at 35 cm instead of metre-scale diamonds, and the service-bath floor uses a newly downloaded CC0 stone tile at its true 2.2 m repeat.

![Master bath after the pass](reports/realism/tour_after3/bath_s.png)

**Blender and the new asset**

I added a narra `aparador` to [build_furniture.py](scripts/build_furniture.py): 2.09 × 0.69 × 1.09 m, 4,232 triangles, turned front legs, fielded doors proud of their stiles, two drawers with four brass pulls, a moulded cornice and a marble slab. Blender 4.2 rebuilt [furniture.glb](public/assets/models/furniture.glb) headless to 32 pieces / 55,864 triangles. It is placed against the dining room's long wall, and the plates and bottles are now positioned off the piece's own footprint instead of the room centre line.

The new material is Poly Haven `grey_tiles` (CC0, Amal Kumar, 2.2 m), fetched into `public/assets/textures/grey_tiles/` and recorded in [ASSET_LICENSES.md](ASSET_LICENSES.md). Source and licence: [polyhaven.com/a/grey_tiles](https://polyhaven.com/a/grey_tiles), [CC0](https://polyhaven.com/license).

**Verification (live renderer, real player spawn path)**

Boot has no page errors beyond the expected pointer-lock refusal. Dining renders at 51 fps / 350 draw calls / 1.248 M triangles, bath at 45 fps / 293 draws, so the lamps and new furniture cost no draw calls. Furniture loads 32 templates with zero missing props. `scripts/drawer_test.cjs` opened all five functional cabinets through the real interact path — 0.30 m travel, closed again, player not pushed, letter/photograph/ledger page collected. Before/after captures used the new [realism_tour.cjs](scripts/realism_tour.cjs); the full write-up is [REALISM_PASS.md](reports/realism/REALISM_PASS.md).

**What this pass did not achieve**

Shadows remain disabled for the Intel HD 4600 target, so there are no contact shadows — the single largest remaining realism limit. Ceilings are still plain dark soffits with no visible beams or cornice, wall finishes stay in one plaster/blue-plaster family with no wainscot or dado, and furniture averages about 1.7k triangles per piece; the kitchen carcasses still read as flat boxes at distance. Room layouts remain the generic dresser rather than an authored plan. All measurements are headless Chromium on this machine, not on the target GPU. # SILID — MASTER MANSION EXTERIOR DESIGN AND RECONSTRUCTION PLAN

Create a convincing, highly detailed exterior for SILID's old Filipino mansion, using the following architectural brief.

## Design identity

The mansion is a large, old, remote Filipino ancestral residence, combining traditional bahay-na-bato-inspired elements with the scale of a multi-storey mansion.

It must look like a real building that was designed, constructed, inhabited, and later neglected. Do not create a generic European castle, fantasy palace, or modern luxury home.

## Required structure

Create a coherent exterior with:
- A prominent central entrance and covered porch.
- A substantial masonry or concrete lower structure.
- Four visible storeys, with the uppermost floor integrated beneath the roofline where appropriate.
- A large central roof and connected secondary roof sections.
- Tall windows with timber frames and capiz-inspired details.
- Deep eaves, window sills, rain protection, gutters, and downpipes.
- A balcony overlooking the main entrance.
- Side wings and projecting rooms that connect logically to the interior.
- A rear service wing and terrace where appropriate.
- Believable foundations, wall thickness, floor edges, and supporting columns.
- A basement and underground areas that connect to the existing building structure.

The exterior must correspond to the actual interior floor plan. Do not create fake windows, balconies, doors, or roof openings that lead into empty space.

## Front facade

Make the main entrance the defining visual feature. Use aged hardwood double doors, a covered porch, substantial masonry supports, tall windows, a balcony, and a layered roof silhouette.

Keep the composition imposing but architecturally believable. Use consistent proportions, real structural connections, and restrained decorative detailing.

## Side and rear facades

The sides must reveal the building's depth and functional layout. Include coherent window arrangements, corridors or verandas where appropriate, believable drainage, and properly connected wings.

The rear should have a more neglected appearance, with a plausible service entrance, utility doors, drainage features, an overgrown courtyard, and connections to the kitchen or basement where the interior design supports them.

## Materials

Research and use appropriate, legally usable PBR materials from resources such as:
- https://polyhaven.com/textures
- https://ambientcg.com/

Use aged plaster, concrete, masonry, old hardwood, weathered roof materials, realistic glass, and restrained metal corrosion.

Apply subtle tropical weathering: rain streaks, damp discoloration, moss in suitable shaded locations, worn paint, dirty window sills, and accumulated debris.

Use correct UVs, texture scale, roughness, normal maps, and material color spaces. Do not use one texture for the entire building.

## Windows and roof

Create properly framed windows with believable thickness, sills, shutters, capiz-inspired panels, and ventanillas where appropriate.

Construct a layered roof with connected ridges, hips, valleys, overhangs, gutters, and ridge caps. Ensure the roof actually covers the building and aligns with the interior ceilings and attic.

Avoid floating roof pieces, flat roof textures pretending to be geometry, and decorative elements with no structural purpose.

## Grounds and approach

The mansion must be at least 30 metres from the nearest road edge.

Create a continuous walkable path from the roadside toward the gate and main entrance. Include natural soil, gravel, fallen leaves, exposed roots, appropriate tropical plants, and believable terrain transitions.

Add a weathered gate and perimeter wall if consistent with the layout. The mansion should be visible from a plausible viewpoint on the road, then grow more imposing as the player approaches.

Do not teleport the player, abruptly reveal the mansion through a scripted position change, or create inaccessible vegetation barriers.

## Nighttime presentation

Preserve SILID's psychological horror atmosphere. Use restrained moonlight, deep shadows, a few warm-lit windows, and realistic illumination from the car headlights and flashlight.

The exterior must remain recognizable in darkness. Do not use black materials to hide geometry defects.

## Integration and validation

Inspect the existing Three.js + Vite project before editing. Preserve the current interior, story, interactions, and opening sequence.

Use the existing Blender assets where appropriate. Back up affected files and assets before making changes.

Verify that:
- The exterior matches the actual interior layout.
- Every visible door and window corresponds to a plausible space.
- The roof and balconies are structurally connected.
- Floor edges and foundations have believable thickness.
- The player can follow the approach path to the entrance.
- The car, road, terrain, and mansion blend together naturally.
- The environment remains performant on an Intel HD Graphics 4600 with 8 GB RAM.

Deliver actual updated assets, a list of modified files, material sources and licenses, and genuine screenshots from the running game.

Do not claim completion based solely on code generation or a successful build. Test the exterior in the running game and report unresolved issues honestly.

Final standard: an imposing, realistic, aged Filipino mansion surrounded by a remote tropical landscape, with coherent architecture, convincing materials, a memorable silhouette, and a believable connection to the road and gameplay.

# SILID — REALISTIC MANSION DOOR SYSTEM
## Main Entrance, Interior Doors, Room-Specific Designs, Functional Hinges, Locks, and Horror Interactions

### OBJECTIVE

Inspect and improve the actual doors throughout the existing SILID Three.js + Vite game. Create a coherent, realistic door system appropriate for an abandoned, wealthy old Filipino mansion.

Do not simply replace every door with a cube or reuse one identical door model everywhere. The main entrance, bedrooms, formal rooms, service rooms, basement, and secret passages must have distinct but architecturally consistent designs.

Preserve the existing mansion layout, story, player controls, collision system, interaction system, inventory, enemy AI, lighting, and performance optimizations.

Before editing, inspect the actual project structure and back up affected files and assets.

### 1. MAIN ENTRANCE

Build a large, imposing pair of solid hardwood entrance doors.

Design requirements:
- Two separate door leaves with realistic thickness and proportions.
- Deep recessed panels, raised wooden moldings, and subtle traditional detailing.
- Dark, aged hardwood resembling old narra or mahogany without claiming a specific wood species if the texture is generic.
- Detailed wood grain, worn varnish, scratches, chipped edges, dust, and restrained moisture damage.
- Separate handles, escutcheons, hinges, and a plausible central locking mechanism.
- A thick wooden frame installed within the actual masonry entrance.
- A stone or concrete threshold and entrance steps that align with the porch and floor.
- Appropriate gaps around the leaves so the doors do not intersect when opened.
- A believable double-door opening sequence.

The entrance must look like part of a large old Filipino ancestral mansion, not a European castle, modern hotel, or fantasy palace.

The door opening must reveal the real foyer behind it. Do not create a fake opening with empty space, a solid wall behind the doorway, or a teleport transition.

### 2. ROOM AND INTERIOR DOORS

Create a reusable door-construction system with separate visual configurations.

A. Formal rooms:
- Taller, detailed wooden panels.
- Darker timber and more elaborate molding.
- Antique brass or dark iron hardware.

B. Bedrooms:
- Single-leaf solid hardwood doors.
- Two to four appropriately proportioned recessed panels.
- A realistic handle, latch, hinges, and frame.

C. Bathrooms:
- Simpler construction and privacy latch.
- Appropriate clearance and privacy-oriented design.

D. Kitchen, pantry, storage, and service rooms:
- Practical, less ornate doors.
- Worn surfaces and functional latches.
- More utilitarian frames and hardware.

E. Library, study, and important locked rooms:
- Distinctive woodwork or hardware appropriate to their narrative importance.
- Keyholes and locks that correspond to actual gameplay mechanics.

F. Basement and generator room:
- A sturdy utility door appropriate to the actual opening and building construction.
- Realistic metal or timber construction; do not use a generic metal slab without a frame, hinges, and handle.

G. Secret rooms and hidden passages:
- Concealed panels, disguised shelving, or believable hidden entrances only where the architecture and story support them.
- The concealed entrance must actually open into a connected, traversable room or passage.

### 3. REAL GEOMETRY AND MATERIALS

Construct the doors using appropriate geometry rather than a single flat plane.

Where visible and affordable, model:
- Door leaves and edges.
- Raised and recessed panels.
- Molding.
- Door frames and jambs.
- Hinges.
- Handles and keyholes.
- Locks and latches.
- Thresholds.
- Transoms or ventilation panels only where appropriate.

Use PBR-compatible materials and efficient textures. Share materials and reusable geometry when possible. Apply believable wear rather than excessive scratches everywhere.

Ensure that the door thickness, frame depth, wall opening, hinge positions, and pivot points agree with one another.

Do not allow floating handles, intersecting panels, paper-thin doors, oversized knobs, missing frames, or decorative details that penetrate the wall.

Use the project's existing asset and material pipeline where practical. If Blender is available and working, it may be used to create or improve the models. Do not assume Blender integration works without testing it.

### 4. FUNCTIONAL DOOR INTERACTIONS

Every functional door must have an explicit state:
- Open or closed.
- Locked or unlocked, when applicable.
- Opening or closing animation state.
- Appropriate persistent state if the game's existing systems support it.

Implement actual hinge-based rotation around the correct side of the frame. Do not rotate a door around its center or slide a hinged door sideways.

Requirements:
- Player interaction opens and closes doors naturally.
- Doors swing in a direction consistent with the room layout and available clearance.
- The main entrance supports its intended double-door behavior.
- Door leaves do not clip through walls, furniture, stairs, or one another.
- The player cannot pass through a closed, solid door.
- Collision is updated appropriately as the door opens and closes.
- The interaction prompt appears only when the player is close enough and facing the relevant door.
- Locked doors display an appropriate message and require the correct key, puzzle, or story condition.
- Locking and unlocking must use the existing inventory and interaction systems.
- Door sounds respond to the action: latch, handle, creak, heavy movement, and closing impact.
- Avoid playing sounds repeatedly every frame.
- Prevent rapid repeated interactions from breaking the animation or state.
- Preserve door state consistently with the existing save or game-state architecture.

Do not make every door locked. Ordinary rooms should remain accessible unless the story or a valid obstacle gives a reason otherwise.

### 5. SILID HORROR GAMEPLAY

Doors should support tension without unfairly obstructing the player.

Where compatible with the existing enemy AI:
- Opening a door can create a restrained creaking sound.
- Closing a door can create a quieter or louder sound depending on the action.
- The enemy may respond to sound only through the existing AI perception system.
- A closed door must not automatically make the player invisible to the enemy unless the game has a deliberate, tested rule for that.
- Locked doors must have a readable explanation or discoverable clue when they block meaningful progression.
- Do not let the enemy, player, or camera become trapped inside a door or doorway.
- Do not allow a door animation to permanently block the only route needed to finish the game.

Optional mechanics such as peeking through a narrow opening or cautiously opening a door should be added only if they integrate cleanly with the current player controller and interaction system.

### 6. ARCHITECTURAL VALIDATION

Inspect every existing door in the mansion, including all four floors, basement, utility spaces, and any implemented tunnels.

For every door, verify:
- It is located in a real wall opening.
- It connects the intended spaces.
- Its dimensions suit the doorway and player.
- The frame is aligned with the wall.
- It does not overlap stairs, floors, ceilings, or furniture.
- It has enough swing clearance.
- It does not block an intended escape route.
- Its collision matches its visible geometry.
- It opens into a real room or passage, not empty space.
- Any stairs behind it have a valid landing and sufficient headroom.

Do not move major walls or redesign the mansion arbitrarily just to fit a door. Adjust the door or opening carefully and preserve the intended architecture.

### 7. PERFORMANCE

SILID must remain playable on modest integrated graphics.

Use shared materials, instancing where appropriate, sensible polygon counts, and efficient collision shapes. Keep small hardware details inexpensive. Avoid excessive real-time shadows and numerous unique high-resolution textures.

The doors should look convincing at normal first-person inspection distance without making the entire mansion expensive to render.

### 8. REQUIRED TESTS

After implementation:
1. Start the actual Vite development server and resolve any build or runtime errors.
2. Test the main entrance from both sides.
3. Open, close, and collide with representative bedroom, formal-room, bathroom, utility, and locked doors.
4. Test keys and locks using the real inventory system.
5. Check every accessible floor and intended basement connection.
6. Test enemy behavior around doors if AI integration is supported.
7. Confirm that no required route or objective becomes inaccessible.
8. Run existing verification scripts and relevant tests.
9. Report which files and assets changed, which tests passed, and any remaining limitations.

Do not claim that a door is functional merely because it looks correct. Verify its actual geometry, collision, animation, and interaction in the running game.

export function buildFacade(scene, arch) {
  const B = buckets();

  // The attic is the exception: its openings are framed by the mansard's

  // a 0.6 m deep tunnel of mouldings.
  for (const win of arch.windows) {

    if (!level || win.level === 'F4') continue;
    dressing(win, level, B);
    // the principal south and east windows are shell-screened; the rear and

The door system is in the live game: 67 leaves with six distinct constructions, real hinges, working locks and paired entrance doors that reveal the actual foyer. The pass also uncovered why the main entrance looked blocked — two facade placement bugs were stacking stone geometry in front of it.

**The entrance** ([architecture.js](src/world/architecture.js)) is now a pair of 2.2 m leaves, each hinged on its own jamb, with four raised panels, face frames, brass ring pulls, escutcheons, three hinges per leaf and a 6 mm meeting gap inside the existing stone portal. It opens inward onto the foyer and stair. Door height was left at the plan's 2.15 m rather than moving the wall cut, casing and facade lintel.

![Paired entrance, closed](reports/doors/entrance_closed.png)

![The pair open onto the foyer and stair](reports/doors/entrance_open_center.png)

**Every other opening** chooses a construction from the rooms it serves: 28 formal, 17 bedroom, 10 service, 9 basement utility, 2 bath and the entrance pair. Service leaves are boarded with iron levers, keyholes and kick plates; bathrooms get a single panel and privacy slide; bedroom and formal leaves get brass knobs and escutcheons. Hinges are three cast plates and a knuckle on the hinged edge. The old leaf gave all geometry groups one walnut material, so its "brass" was painted wood; each leaf now carries wood and metal materials, with a new procedural `wroughtIron` for the service ironmongery.

![Hardware, meeting stile and hinges](reports/doors/entrance_hardware.png)

![Bedroom leaf open into the furnished room](reports/doors/bedroom_open.png)

**Two facade bugs were burying the entrance.** Every pilaster was built at the wall's centre because its `at` station was never applied, so the whole south elevation's pilasters stacked into one full-height shaft in front of the doors. Every window dressing had the same omission, putting a window's stone jambs and sill across the entrance. [facade.js](src/world/facade.js) now slides both to their real stations. This changes all elevations; only the south face has been re-shot so far.

**Gameplay preserved and extended.** Both entrance leaves animate together, including when the Resident forces the door. Closing is refused while you stand in the opening ("Step clear of the doorway first."), which prevents the leaf collider trapping the player. Locks still use the existing brass key and F3 study predicate. New `latch()` and heavier entrance `creak()` sounds play once per action, and the creak now feeds the existing `noise()` → `Resident.hear()` channel at 3.2 m for interior doors and 5.5 m for the entrance.

**Verification**, all against the running game at `?probe=1`:

- [doors_probe.cjs](scripts/doors_probe.cjs): 67 doors, **0** collider/opening mismatches, **0** thin leaves, **0** duplicate keys, **0** blocked swing arcs. Representative doors were opened and closed through the real prompt: entrance from both sides (1.35/−1.35, collider off, centre passable, back to 0.01 and solid), bedroom, formal room, basement; the F3 study refuses without the key with the correct message and opens with it.

- Resident hearing: 1.3 m → `investigate` at the door; 6.1 m → stays `patrol`.

# SILID — REPLACE INSPECT-ONLY FEATURES WITH REAL, PHYSICAL INTERACTIONS

## PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Audit and overhaul the interaction system throughout the existing SILID game.

I do NOT want inspect-only interactions such as:
- "Inspect Aparador"
- "Inspect Console"
- "Inspect Drawer"
- "Inspect Bed"
- "Inspect Cabinet"
- "Inspect Object"

These interactions are not sufficient. I want the player to perform meaningful actions directly on actual 3D objects in the game world.

**The core rule: if an object is presented as interactable, interacting with it must perform a real, appropriate action—not merely display a description, open an inspection panel, zoom a camera, or show text.**

Do not rebuild the entire project from scratch. Inspect the existing Three.js + Vite codebase first, identify the current interaction architecture, back up affected files, and preserve the existing player controller, inventory, story, enemy AI, puzzles, and game state.

## 1. REMOVE INSPECT-ONLY INTERACTION PROMPTS

Find all existing inspect-only actions, prompts, and handlers across the project.

Replace them with contextual actions that correspond to the actual object and its function.

Examples:
- "Inspect Aparador" → "Open Aparador" or "Open Drawer"
- "Inspect Console" → "Use Console" or a specific control action supported by the console
- "Inspect Bed" → "Hide Under Bed" or "Use Bed", depending on the actual interaction
- "Inspect Cabinet" → "Open Cabinet"
- "Inspect Locker" → "Open Locker"
- "Inspect Door" → "Open Door"
- "Inspect Generator" → "Repair Generator", "Start Generator", or "Use Generator", depending on its current state.

Do not blindly rename every prompt. Implement the actual underlying behavior.

Remove generic inspection panels wherever they substitute for the intended gameplay. A short contextual message is acceptable when it communicates the result of a real action, explains why an action is unavailable, or delivers necessary story information.

## 2. MAKE STORAGE FURNITURE PHYSICALLY FUNCTIONAL

### Aparadors and cabinets

An aparador must be a proper piece of furniture, not a decorative box with an inspection prompt.

Implement:
- Real cabinet doors that rotate around hinges.
- Actual drawers that slide outward along their rails.
- Visible handles and plausible interior cavities.
- Shelves and compartments where appropriate.
- Contents positioned inside the actual compartments.
- Opening and closing animations.
- Collision and clearance that prevent the player from walking through solid furniture.
- Contextual interaction prompts that update according to the object's state.

For example, when Del opens a drawer, the drawer must visibly slide out. If it contains a key, the key must be physically present inside the drawer and collectible through the existing inventory system.

When a drawer is empty, opening it should reveal an empty compartment—not a generic inspection message.

Cabinet doors and drawers must not clip through each other, the wall, or nearby furniture. Do not allow multiple rapid interactions to corrupt their positions or states.

### Lockers and wardrobes

Implement real doors, handles, interiors, and storage compartments. Where hiding is supported by the game design, provide a deliberate hiding interaction with suitable animation, player positioning, camera behavior, and exit controls.

A wardrobe that is merely decorative must not advertise itself as usable storage or hiding space.

## 3. MAKE OBJECTS PERFORM THEIR ACTUAL FUNCTIONS

Implement object-specific actions wherever the object exists and the function makes sense.

| Object | Required real interaction |
|---|---|
| Aparador | Open cabinet doors and drawers; retrieve actual contents |
| Drawer | Slide open and closed; reveal or retrieve contents |
| Wardrobe | Open doors; hide inside if designed and tested for hiding |
| Locker | Open, close, unlock, and hide if supported |
| Bed | Hide underneath where there is physical clearance; allow peeking and exiting |
| Door | Open and close on hinges; unlock with valid keys when applicable |
| Telephone | Pick up, use, dial, or trigger a meaningful story event if supported by its design |
| Radio | Turn on and off; operate tuning or volume controls if implemented |
| Console | Press actual buttons or operate actual switches that produce corresponding effects |
| Generator | Perform real repair and startup steps using required tools or components |
| Fuse box | Open its cover; insert, remove, or replace compatible fuses where gameplay requires |
| Light switch | Toggle the corresponding light or circuit |
| Sink or faucet | Operate the tap and trigger an appropriate response if included in gameplay |
| Kitchen cabinets | Open actual doors and drawers; access supported contents |
| Containers | Open or unlock them; reveal their real contents |
| Puzzle mechanism | Operate the relevant controls and update the actual puzzle state |
| Secret entrance | Activate its real mechanism and open a connected passage |
| Well or pump | Operate it only if a real gameplay purpose and corresponding state exist |

These are examples, not permission to invent unrelated mechanics or add every listed feature indiscriminately. Inspect the existing story and object models. Implement functions that fit SILID's world and gameplay.

## 4. THE CONSOLE MUST BE A REAL DEVICE

Investigate what the current in-game console actually represents before changing it.

If it is an electrical or control console:
- Model the actual controls, buttons, switches, indicators, and relevant panels.
- Allow the player to activate the appropriate controls.
- Make each control affect a real game state, device, puzzle, or system.
- Show feedback through the device itself: indicator lights, movement, sound, or a state change.
- If the console requires power, reflect that dependency.
- If a control cannot be used, communicate the actual reason.

Do not leave the console as a decorative box with an "Inspect Console" prompt.

If the current console is only a placeholder without a defined function, inspect the story and surrounding systems first. Assign a function only when it fits the established design.

## 5. FIRST-PERSON INTERACTION AND FEEDBACK

Use the existing first-person controller and interaction framework.

When the player looks at a usable object within interaction range:
1. Identify the specific object or component being targeted.
2. Display its available contextual action.
3. Let the player trigger the action using the established interaction input.
4. Perform the action on the actual 3D object.
5. Update the object's state, collision, inventory, puzzle state, or other affected system.
6. Provide appropriate visual and audio feedback.
7. Update the prompt to reflect the new state.

Examples:
- A closed drawer displays "Open Drawer"; once open, it displays "Close Drawer".
- A locked cabinet displays "Unlock Cabinet" only when the player can perform that action, or explains the missing requirement.
- A running generator displays its current operational state rather than continuing to offer a repair action.
- A collected item disappears from its original location and enters the real inventory.

Do not rely on floating text or inspection overlays as a substitute for these actions.

## 6. SUPPORT MULTIPLE INTERACTABLE COMPONENTS ON ONE OBJECT

An aparador may have two doors and several drawers. The player must be able to target individual components when appropriate.

Implement stable component-level interaction targets so the player can:
- Open the left drawer without automatically opening every other drawer.
- Open the right cabinet door independently when the design allows it.
- Target a handle, switch, button, or lock when that component needs a separate action.

Avoid duplicate prompts, ambiguous targets, and interactions that activate the wrong object.

If precise targeting is impractical for a particular object, provide a clear, intentional interaction that operates the correct component. Do not make the player fight the targeting system.

## 7. HIDING, PEEKING, AND ENEMY CONSEQUENCES

For beds, wardrobes, lockers, and other designated hiding places, implement real hiding mechanics where supported.

The player must enter the correct physical hiding position, have a suitable camera position, and be able to peek and exit through deliberate controls.

Hiding must not:
- Teleport the player into arbitrary coordinates.
- Leave the player stuck in furniture.
- Allow walking through solid geometry.
- Make the player automatically invisible under every circumstance.

Integrate visibility, noise, and enemy detection with the existing AI where feasible. Any hiding protection must follow explicit, testable gameplay rules.

## 8. INTERACTION STATE, INVENTORY, AND PUZZLE CONSISTENCY

Every functional object must have a defined state model.

Examples include:
- Drawer: open or closed.
- Cabinet: individual doors open or closed.
- Lock: locked or unlocked.
- Generator: unrepaired, repaired, or running, as appropriate to the existing design.
- Fuse box: cover state, installed fuse state, and power state where applicable.
- Item: present, collected, or consumed when the established game mechanics permit consumption.
- Console: current operating state and valid control states.

Integrate these states with existing systems instead of creating competing inventory or game-state implementations.

Preserve important state changes when required by the existing save architecture. Make interactions idempotent where necessary so repeated inputs do not duplicate items, reset animations, or corrupt object positions.

Required progression items must remain obtainable. Apply SILID's solvability rules: validate generated runs, ensure required items are reachable, avoid circular item dependencies, and preserve valid paths to generator repair and escape.

## 9. REMOVE MISLEADING INTERACTABLES

Audit the entire mansion and exterior.

Every object must be classified as one of:
- **Functional interactable:** has a real action and a defined result.
- **Decorative scenery:** does not advertise an interaction.
- **Story object:** triggers a deliberate narrative event through a real interaction.
- **Blocked or unavailable object:** communicates a truthful reason when the player attempts an action.

Do not put "Inspect" prompts on every object just to make the environment seem interactive.

Do not label every decorative object as usable. Conversely, do not leave meaningful story or gameplay objects with only an inspection description when a real action is expected.

## 10. TEST THE RUNNING GAME

After implementation:
- Start the real Vite development server.
- Test representative aparadors, individual drawers, cabinet doors, wardrobes, beds, the telephone, console, generator, fuse box, and normal doors.
- Verify opening, closing, collision, item collection, inventory updates, puzzle effects, and state changes.
- Verify that prompts accurately reflect each object's current state.
- Check the browser console for runtime errors.
- Run existing verification scripts and relevant tests.
- Confirm that the game remains responsive on modest integrated graphics.

Do not report an interaction as implemented merely because its prompt changed or an animation played. Verify that the intended gameplay result actually occurs.

At completion, provide a concise report of the actual files changed, the functional interactions implemented, the tests performed, and any interactions that remain unfinished.

**Final acceptance criterion:** SILID must feel like a physical world Del can operate—not a collection of objects that only display inspection text.

function rug(d, room, w = 3, h = 2.2) {
  // A rug is a plane: over the stairwell it would hang in the air across the
  // drop (it did, on every floor of the stair hall). Keep the centre clear of
  // the stair hole by choosing the quadrant of the room with the most room.
  const fits = (cx, cz, ww, hh) => Math.min(cx - room.x0 - ww / 2, room.x1 - cx - ww / 2,
    cz - room.z0 - hh / 2, room.z1 - cz - hh / 2) >= 0.3;
  let bx = (room.x0 + room.x1) / 2, bz = (room.z0 + room.z1) / 2;
  if (Math.hypot(bx - STAIR.cx, bz - STAIR.cz) < STAIR.holeR + Math.hypot(w, h) / 2 + 0.35) {
    let placed = false;
    for (const scale of [1, 0.62]) {
      const ww = w * scale, hh = h * scale;
      const clear = STAIR.holeR + Math.hypot(ww, hh) / 2 + 0.3;
      let best = -1, bcx = 0, bcz = 0;
      for (const fx of [0.3, 0.7, 0.5, 0.2, 0.8]) {
        for (const fz of [0.3, 0.7, 0.5, 0.2, 0.8]) {
          const cx = room.x0 + (room.x1 - room.x0) * fx;
          const cz = room.z0 + (room.z1 - room.z0) * fz;
          if (!fits(cx, cz, ww, hh)) continue;
          const score = Math.hypot(cx - STAIR.cx, cz - STAIR.cz);
          if (score > best) { best = score; bcx = cx; bcz = cz; }
        }
      }
      if (best >= clear) { bx = bcx; bz = bcz; w = ww; h = hh; placed = true; break; }
    }
    if (!placed) return;   // no clear floor here: no rug at all
  }
  const g = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(w, h, 1, 1);
  g.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
  const uv = g.attributes.uv;
  for (let i = 0; i < uv.count; i++) uv.setXY(i, uv.getX(i) * w, uv.getY(i) * h);
  g.translate(bx, d.y + 0.012, bz);
  d.geo('rug', g);
}

function portrait(d, room, wall, offset, w = 0.7, h = 0.95, y = 1.75) {
  // The frame stands 12 mm proud of the plaster, wherever the plaster actually
  // is: an exterior wall's face is 0.21 m inside the drawn room line.
  const alongX = wall === 'N' || wall === 'S';
  const axis = alongX ? 'x' : 'z';
  const line = alongX ? (wall === 'N' ? room.z1 : room.z0) : (wall === 'W' ? room.x0 : room.x1);
  const dir = (wall === 'N' || wall === 'E') ? -1 : 1;
  const level = d.level;
  const t = wallFace(level, axis, line).half + 0.012;
  let x, z, rot;
  if (wall === 'N') { x = room.x0 + (room.x1 - room.x0) * offset; z = room.z1 - t; rot = Math.PI; }
  else if (wall === 'S') { x = room.x0 + (room.x1 - room.x0) * offset; z = room.z0 + t; rot = 0; }
  else if (wall === 'E') { x = room.x1 - t; z = room.z0 + (room.z1 - room.z0) * offset; rot = -Math.PI / 2; }

  const frame = box(w + 0.09, h + 0.09, 0.045, 1);

  frame.translate(x, d.y + y, z);

  const inner = box(w, h, 0.02, 1);
  inner.rotateY(rot);
  inner.translate(x, d.y + y, z);
  d.geo('marble', inner);
}

Report for the pass that removed the inspect-only layer and made the furniture,
storage and hiding places operate as physical objects.

## The rule applied

An object may only advertise a prompt if pressing E changes something in the
world: a leaf swings on a hinge, a drawer leaves its carcass on its runners, an
item leaves a shelf and enters the inventory, a hiding place accepts the body.
If nothing can be changed, the object is scenery and offers no prompt at all.

The old build had a single `INSPECT` table in `src/world/props.js` (cooker,
fridge, washer, bath, basin, wc, shower) whose only effect was a line of prose —
plus furnishing pieces whose prompt said "Inspect". That layer is gone. The
descriptions that survived are the ones printed *after* a real action, e.g. the
armoire's doors swinging open, or the generator refusing because the tank is dry.

## What is interactable now

`props.interactables` holds 38 entries, plus the 67 door leaves from the door
system. Every kind is an action:

| kind | count | what pressing E does |
|---|---|---|
| door | 67 | swings the leaf on its hinge, disables/enables its collider, locks/unlocks |
| drawer | 13 | slides the drawer body out on its runners; a second press closes it |
| pickup | 8 | hides the world mesh, adds the item to the inventory (phone included) |
| hide |  [… 3,884 characters omitted] ent 0.000.

**Movement and cost** — same runs: 902 colliders, 67 door colliders present,
348 objects, ~690k triangles at 60 fps in the probe view.

**Doors** — `node scripts/doors_probe.cjs`
67 leaves, styles utility 9 / entrance 1 / formal 28 / service 10 / bedroom 17 /
bath 2; levels B1 9, GF 24, F2 14, F3 11, F4 9. `colliderMismatch: []`,
`blockedSwings: []`, `thinLeaves: []`, `duplicateKeys: []`.
Entrance from outside and from the foyer: both leaves reach ±1.35 rad, the
collider disables when open and blocks the centre when closed. Locked study on
F3: first press "Locked. The brass key is upstairs, in the master bedroom.",
opens after the key.

**Power chain** — `node scripts/apparatus_test.cjs`
Fuse panel cover swings to −1.45 rad and reports open; the fuse fits
(`installed: true`, mesh visible); the cover closes to 0. Generator with no fuel
offers its prompt, then powers the house (`powered: true`).

**Screenshots** — `node scripts/interaction_shots.cjs`, in

{"kind":"tool","id":"hnTj3zxCDtA","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"scripts/pickup_probe.cjs","instructions":"Add a probe that takes every world pickup through the real interaction path.","content":"// Pickup probe: every object the world offers as a pickup is taken the way a
// player takes it — stand near it, ask the game what is in reach, press E — and
// the result is checked against the inventory and the visible mesh.
//
// The phone is the one that matters most: it is the story object, it drives the
// hand model and the phone UI, and its world copy has to disappear.
const { chromium } = require('playwright');

const URL = process.env.SILID_URL || 'http://127.0.0.1:5333/?probe=1';

(async () => {
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: true });
  const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1000, height: 620 } });
  const errors = [];
  page.on('pageerror', (e) => errors.push(e.message));
  await page.goto(URL);
  await page.waitForFunction(() => window.__silid?.ready, null, { timeout: 180000 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);

  const out = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const w = window.__silid, g = w.game;
    const rows = [];
    const pickups = w.props.interactables.filter((i) => i.kind === 'pickup');
    for (const p of pickups) {
      let found = null;
      // try eight approaches at arm's length and take the one where the game
      // itself agrees the object is what you are looking at
      for (let a = 0; a < 8 && !found; a++) {
        const th = (a / 8) * Math.PI * 2;
        const px = p.x + Math.sin(th) * 0.75, pz = p.z + Math.cos(th) * 0.75;
        for (const pitch of [-0.55, -0.35, -0.15, 0.05]) {
          w.spawnAt(px, pz, p.y - 1.15, th, pitch);
          g.update(0.05);
          const t = g.nearestInteraction();
          if (t && t.kind === 'pickup' && t.id === p.id) { found = t; break; }
        }
      }
      if (!found) { rows.push({ id: p.id, name: p.name, reached: false }); continue; }
      const before = g.inventory.size;
      const prompt = document.getElementById('prompt')?.textContent || '';
      g.interact();
      g.update(0.05);
      const mesh = w.scene.getObjectByName('phone_world') || null;
      rows.push({
        id: p.id, name: p.name, reached: true, prompt,
        gained: g.inventory.size === before + 1,
        inInventory: g.inventory.has(p.id),
        worldHidden: p.mesh ? p.mesh.visible === false : null,
        phoneHeld: p.id === 'phone' ? !!g.phoneHeld : undefined,
        after: document.getElementById('prompt')?.textContent || '',
        worldPhoneVisible: mesh ? mesh.visible : undefined,
      });
    }
    return {
      rows,
      pageErrors: [],
      phoneUi: !!document.getElementById('phone'),
      inventory: [...g.inventory],
    };

{"kind":"tool","id":"hnuIG8ioFVM","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"scripts/phone_hand_probe.cjs","instructions":"Add a probe verifying the phone model enters the player's hand after pickup.","content":"// Phone hand check: take the phone through the pickup path and confirm the
// modelled asset actually enters the player's hand (not just the inventory).
// The GLB loads asynchronously, so the check waits for it rather than reading
// the flag on the same frame as the keypress.
const { chromium } = require('playwright');
const fs = require('fs');

const URL = process.env.SILID_URL || 'http://127.0.0.1:5333/?probe=1';
const OUT = 'reports/interactions/shots';

(async () => {
  fs.mkdirSync(OUT, { recursive: true });
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: true });
  const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1100, height: 680 } });
  const errors = [];
  page.on('pageerror', (e) => errors.push(e.message));
  await page.goto(URL);
  await page.waitForFunction(() => window.__silid?.ready, null, { timeout: 180000 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);

  const taken = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const w = window.__silid, g = w.game;
    const p = w.props.interactables.find((i) => i.id === 'phone');
    if (!p) return { found: false };
    let hit = null;
    for (let a = 0; a < 8 && !hit; a++) {
      const th = (a / 8) * Math.PI * 2;
      for (const pitch of [-0.55, -0.35, -0.15, 0.05]) {
        w.spawnAt(p.x + Math.sin(th) * 0.75, p.z + Math.cos(th) * 0.75, p.y - 1.15, th, pitch);
        g.update(0.05);
        const t = g.nearestInteraction();
        if (t && t.kind === 'pickup' && t.id === 'phone') { hit = { prompt: document.getElementById('prompt')?.textContent }; break; }
      }
    }
    if (!hit) return { found: true, reached: false };
    g.interact();
    return { found: true, reached: true, prompt: hit.prompt, inInventory: g.inventory.has('phone') };
  });

  // the phone model is loaded on demand; give the loader time
  const held = await page.waitForFunction(() => {
    const g = window.__silid.game;
    return !!(g.heldPhone && g.heldPhoneGroup);
  }, null, { timeout: 20000 }).then(() => true).catch(() => false);

  const state = await page.evaluate(() => {
    const g = window.__silid.game;
    return {
      held: !!g.heldPhone,
      heldGroupVisible: g.heldPhoneGroup ? g.heldPhoneGroup.visible : null,
      phoneMeshes: g.heldPhoneGroup ? (() => { let n = 0; g.heldPhoneGroup.traverse((o) => { if (o.isMesh) n++; }); return n; })() : 0,
    };
  });

  // look at the hand for the photograph
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    const w = window.__silid;
    w.game.player.pitch = -0.45;
    w.game.update(0.05);
  });
  const cdp = await page.context().newCDPSession(page);
  const { data } = await cdp.send('Page.captureScreenshot', { format: 'png' });
  fs.writeFileSync(`${OUT}/06_phone_in_hand.png`, Buffer.from(data, 'base64'));

  console.log(JSON.stringify({ taken, held, state, pageErrors: errors }, null, 1));
  await browser.close();
})().catch((e) => { console.error(e); process.exit(1); });
"}}

All prompts that only described an object are gone, and the furniture they pointed at now does the thing it looks like it should do.

**What changed in behaviour**

- `props.interactables` is down to 34 entries plus 67 door leaves, and every kind is an action: `door`, `drawer`, `pickup`, `hide`, `hidedoor`, `trap`, `cupboard`, `cabinetItem`, `fusebox`, `generator`, `read`. No `inspect` kind survives anywhere in `src`.
- A drawer slides 0.30 m out on its runners, exposes a real cavity between separate front, sides and bottom, and only offers "search" if something is actually inside. Aim is scored in 3-D, so the vertical component picks *which* drawer in a column you open.
- The aparador is two actions at two heights: the handle line swings both leaves (±1.35 rad) on their hinges; only then does the cavity offer "hide inside", which steps the camera in and gives "peek out / Q leave" — with noise emitted on entry and on peek, so hiding is not invisibility.
- Kitchen and pantry cupboards open both leaves on hinges and reveal shelving with the tin and the recipe card standing on it, each takeable into the real inventory.
- Fuse panel: cover to −1.45 rad, fuse fits visibly, cover closes, generator then takes fuel and powers the house.
- The player's phone is taken through the same pickup path and appears as the modelled GLB in the hand, lock screen lit, not a flat overlay.

![Drawer pulled out](reports/interactions/shots/01_dresser_drawer.png)

![Cupboard open with its contents](reports/interactions/shots/02_kitchen_cupboard.png)

**Two real defects the audit caught and I fixed**

1. The dressing pass runs per room, and three rooms share the `foyer` kind and three share `workshop` — so the world contained three handsets and three ceramic fuses with the same ids. After taking the first, the other two stayed visible and inert. The phone is now dressed in the ground-floor foyer only, the fuse on the basement bench only: 8 pickup entries → 4 unique ones.
2. A phone picked up before its GLB finished loading went into the inventory with an empty fist and never recovered. `_loadPhoneAsync()` now completes that deferred pickup when the asset resolves.

![Phone in hand after pickup](reports/interactions/shots/06_phone_in_hand.png)

**Verification actually run against the dev server**

- `interactions_probe.cjs` — no page errors, no fails, armoire `hide → peek → out`, under-bed `get under → out`, both cupboards' hinges and items.
- `drawer_test.cjs` — five units, 0.300 m travel each, contents taken, closed again, residual 0, player displacement 0.
- `pickup_probe.cjs` — fuel, fuse, phone, key reachable and taken; inventory ends `[fuel, fuse, phone, key]`.
- `phone_hand_probe.cjs` — `heldPhone` true, group visible, 4 meshes.
- `doors_probe.cjs` — 67 leaves, `colliderMismatch: []`, `blockedSwings: []`; entrance pairs ±1.35, locked study opens with the brass key.
- `apparatus_test.cjs` — fuse panel and generator chain, `powered: true`.

Full write-up with file list, measurements and limits: [REPORT.md](reports/interactions/REPORT.md).

**Limits, stated plainly**

SILID has no telephone, radio or electrical console device in the world — the only powered props are the generator and fuse panel, so I did not invent one; kitchen and bathroom appliances are scenery and no longer advertise a prompt. There is no save system, so object states last the session. The phone GLB takes about 18 s to decode under software rendering, so the deferred pickup path is what covers the first seconds of a run.

Next, the interaction layer would benefit from a save/restore of object state and a solvability re-check now that only one phone and one fuse exist.

function foundationPlanting(B, gf) {
  const fp = gf.footprint;
  const rnd = prng(4021);
  const faces = [
    { axis: 'x', line: fp.z1, out: 1, a: fp.x0, b: fp.x1 },
    { axis: 'x', line: fp.z0, out: -1, a: fp.x0, b: fp.x1 },
    { axis: 'z', line: fp.x1, out: 1, a: fp.z0, b: fp.z1 },
    { axis: 'z', line: fp.x0, out: -1, a: fp.z0, b: fp.z1 },
  ];
  for (const f of faces) {
    const yaw0 = f.axis === 'x' ? (f.out > 0 ? 0 : Math.PI) : (f.out > 0 ? Math.PI / 2 : -Math.PI / 2);
    for (let u = f.a + 0.5; u < f.b - 0.5; u += 1.05 + rnd() * 0.85) {
      // the approach is kept open: nothing grows across the entrance bay
      if (f.axis === 'x' && f.out > 0 && u > -6.2 && u < 6.2) continue;
      let onDoor = false;
      for (const d of gf.doors) {
        if (d.axis !== f.axis || Math.abs(d.c - f.line) > 0.02) continue;
        if (Math.abs(u - d.at) < d.w / 2 + 1.0) onDoor = true;
      }
      if (onDoor) continue;
      const dist = TE / 2 + 0.42 + rnd() * 0.85;
      const h = 0.55 + rnd() * 0.95;
      for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
        const w = 0.55 + rnd() * 0.65;
        const g = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(w, h * (0.8 + rnd() * 0.35));
        const uv = g.attributes.uv;
        for (let i = 0; i < uv.count; i++) uv.setXY(i, uv.getX(i) * w, uv.getY(i) * h);
        const yaw = yaw0 + (k - 1) * 0.85 + (rnd() - 0.5) * 0.5;
        g.rotateY(yaw);
        const du = (rnd() - 0.5) * 0.85;
        const dy = h / 2 + 0.02;
        if (f.axis === 'x') g.translate(u + du, dy, f.line + f.out * (dist + rnd() * 0.4));
        else g.translate(f.line + f.out * (dist + rnd() * 0.4), dy, u + du);
        B.ivy.push(g);
      }

  }
}

Do not simply place several disconnected staircase models on top of one another. Do not teleport the player between floors. Do not solve traversal problems by disabling collisions.

- Ground-floor elevation.

- Number of risers per floor.

- Intermediate landing positions.

- Head clearance.

Calculate the riser count and tread layout for each storey. Ensure the top riser connects to the intended floor level and that the final tread does not intersect the floor slab.

### 2. STAIRCASE LAYOUT

Where the existing architecture permits, construct a U-shaped staircase with two flights connected by a broad intermediate landing.

The main staircase should:
- Begin at the ground-floor foyer or central hall.
- Connect naturally to the second-floor landing.
- Continue from the second floor to the third floor.
- Continue from the third floor to the fourth floor.
- Maintain consistent architectural logic and believable proportions.
- Provide enough room for the player to turn, climb, and descend without snagging.
- Connect to genuine upper-floor corridors and rooms.

Align the staircase with the building's actual footprint. Do not force a central staircase into a room where it cannot fit. If the existing layout requires a different orientation, choose the most logical alternative while preserving continuous access.

### 3. BUILD REAL STAIR GEOMETRY

Each flight must have actual:
- Horizontal treads.
- Vertical risers.
- Side stringers or another believable supporting structure.
- A structurally coherent landing.
- Handrails and balusters where appropriate.
- Correct attachment to floors and upper landings.

The steps must have real depth and thickness. Avoid paper-thin slabs, overlapping stair meshes, decorative stair surfaces that float above the collision geometry, or a single sloping ramp disguised as stairs.

Use dark aged hardwood for the treads and handrails, with restrained wear, scratches, and realistic wood grain. Use appropriate supporting materials for the mansion's construction.

Create believable balustrades with properly spaced posts and rails. Keep decorative elements proportionate and do not allow them to obstruct the player's movement.

### 4. FLOOR OPENINGS AND HEAD CLEARANCE

Inspect every floor slab above and below the staircase.

Create correctly sized openings for each flight and landing. The floor must not pass through the staircase, cover the upper steps, or block the player's head.

- Remove floor geometry only where the stairwell opening genuinely requires it.
- Preserve floor slabs everywhere else.
- Ensure the staircase emerges onto each floor at the correct elevation.
- Prevent ceilings, beams, and overhead landings from intersecting the player capsule or camera.
- Ensure the player can walk onto the upper floor without hitting an invisible ceiling or slab.
- Keep railings aligned with the actual edges of the openings.
- Prevent gaps large enough for the player to fall through accidentally.

Do not hide intersections by placing decorative trim over them. Correct the underlying geometry.

### 5. PLAYER COLLISION AND CLIMBING

Integrate the staircase with the existing player movement and collision system.

Test:
- Walking up and down every flight.
- Stepping onto and off each landing.
- Turning around at intermediate landings.
- Walking between the staircase and the upper-floor corridor.
- Descending from the fourth floor to the ground floor.
- Approaching and using doors beside the staircase.
- Moving past railings and nearby furniture.

Do not enlarge collision boxes to the point that they block entire landings or corridors.

### 6. STAIRWELL AND FLOOR CONNECTIONS

All intended routes must remain connected:
- Ground floor to second floor.
- Second floor to third floor.
- Third floor to fourth floor.
- Every stair landing to its intended corridor.

### 7. REALISTIC VISUAL PRESENTATION

- Aged dark hardwood treads and handrails.
- Properly modeled balusters and newel posts.
